Nav employee: Good morning, and welcome. My name is Emma. I will be your caseworker today. We have about an hour set aside. The purpose of the meeting is to talk about your current situation, what kind of work you are looking for, what may be difficult right now, and what kind of follow-up could help you move forward.
Client: Good morning. That sounds fine. I am a little nervous, to be honest. I have not had this kind of meeting before.
Nav employee: That is understandable. We will take it step by step. The goal is not to test you or pressure you. The goal is to understand your situation and agree on realistic next steps. If anything is unclear, just stop me and ask.
Client: Thank you. That helps.
Nav employee: Can you start by telling me why you contacted the unemployment office and how your situation is right now?
Client: I lost my job about two months ago. I worked in a warehouse for almost six years. The company lost a large contract, and several people were laid off. I have been applying for jobs since then, but I have not had much response.
Nav employee: So you were laid off because of changes in the company, not because you chose to leave?
Client: Yes, exactly. It was not something I wanted. I liked the job in many ways, but the company had to reduce staff.
Nav employee: What kind of tasks did you have in the warehouse?
Client: Mostly receiving goods, packing orders, using a handheld scanner, checking inventory, and sometimes driving a forklift. I also helped train new employees because I had been there for a while.
Nav employee: So you have experience with logistics, stock control, packing, warehouse systems, forklift work, and training colleagues.
Client: Yes, I guess so. I do not always think of it that way, but I have done quite a lot.
Nav employee: It is common to underestimate your own experience after losing a job. Part of our work can be to make your skills more visible in your CV and applications. Have you updated your CV after you were laid off?
Client: I changed the dates, but not much else. It still looks like the CV I made several years ago.
Nav employee: Then one possible next step is to improve the CV so it describes your experience more clearly. Before we decide that, I want to understand what kind of work you are looking for. Are you mainly looking for warehouse work again, or are you considering other types of jobs?
Client: I have applied for warehouse jobs and delivery assistant jobs. I know that field, so it feels natural. But I am also unsure. My back has been bothering me, and I am not sure I can continue with heavy lifting every day.
Nav employee: Thank you for saying that. We do not need to go into medical details today, but it is relevant to talk about what kind of tasks are realistic. Do you want to avoid work that is mostly heavy physical lifting?
Client: Yes. I can lift some things, and I can be active, but constant heavy lifting is hard. At my old job there were busy periods where I lifted a lot, and I felt it for days afterward.
Nav employee: Then it makes sense to look for jobs where your logistics experience is useful, but the physical load is lower. For example inventory control, order administration, customer service related to logistics, goods reception, or warehouse coordination.
Client: I have not really thought about those roles. I assumed they required office experience or more education.
Nav employee: Some do, but not all. You already understand warehouse operations. That can be valuable in administrative or coordinating roles. The question is how to present your experience, and whether you need some additional training in office systems, Excel, or customer communication.
Client: I can use a computer, but I am not very confident with Excel. We used a warehouse system at work, but mostly for scanning and checking orders.
Nav employee: That is still relevant. Many jobs use digital systems. If you are open to it, we can look at short courses that strengthen your digital skills. It does not have to be a long education.
Client: I would be open to that. I am just worried about time and money. I need income.
Nav employee: Of course. Income is important. Are you currently receiving unemployment benefits?
Client: I applied for unemployment benefits after I was laid off. I have received some payments, but I am not completely sure how long it lasts or what I have to do to keep receiving it.
Nav employee: We can talk about the general activity requirements. You usually need to be a real jobseeker, register job search activity, send employment status forms when required, and be available for suitable work. If you have questions about specific payments or decisions, we can look at the messages you have received, but today I will focus on your work plan and activity.
Client: That is fine. I have been sending the forms, but I get nervous that I might do something wrong.
Nav employee: Many people feel that way. One agreement from today can be that you check messages and tasks in the online portal once a week, so nothing is missed. We can also write down the main job search activities you will do.
Client: That would help. I like having things written down.
Nav employee: How many jobs have you applied for since you were laid off?
Client: Maybe twelve or thirteen. Mostly warehouse jobs. I also applied for two driver assistant jobs. I got one rejection and no response from the rest.
Nav employee: Have you been invited to any interviews?
Client: No, not yet.
Nav employee: That can be discouraging. Do you send the same application each time, or do you adapt it to each job?
Client: Mostly the same one. I change the company name and a few sentences, but not much more.
Nav employee: That may be one reason you are not getting much response. Employers often look for a clear match between the job advertisement and the application. If the advertisement asks for inventory control, accuracy, forklift experience, or reliability, your application should show examples of those things.
Client: I see. I think my applications have been too general.
Nav employee: That is common, and it can be improved. What do you think is your strongest work experience?
Client: I am reliable. I rarely missed work. I can work quickly without making many mistakes. I also helped new people when they started.
Nav employee: Those are strong points. We can phrase them concretely. For example: six years of warehouse experience, including order picking, inventory checks, forklift driving, and training new employees. That says more than only writing warehouse worker.
Client: Yes, that sounds better.
Nav employee: Do you have a forklift certificate?
Client: Yes, T1, T2, and T4. I got it through the employer.
Nav employee: Excellent. Is that clearly listed in your CV?
Client: I think it is near the bottom, but maybe not very visible.
Nav employee: We should move it higher if you are applying for logistics jobs. Certificates, systems experience, and practical skills should be easy for the employer to find. Have you used specific warehouse software?
Client: It was called Astro WMS. I also used an internal scanning system. I do not know if that matters.
Nav employee: It matters. Even if another company uses a different system, it shows that you are used to digital warehouse tools. Put it in the CV.
Client: Okay.
Nav employee: Let us talk about your job goal. If you could choose a realistic direction for the next six months, what would you prefer?
Client: I would like a job where I still use my warehouse experience, but with less heavy lifting. Maybe inventory, logistics assistant, or something with orders. I am not sure what the job titles are.
Nav employee: That is a good start. We can describe the goal as work in logistics, inventory control, order processing, or other roles where warehouse experience is useful and the physical workload is manageable. Does that sound right?
Client: Yes, that sounds like what I mean.
Nav employee: Are you willing to work full time if the tasks are suitable?
Client: Yes, I want full-time work if I can manage the tasks. I am also open to part time if that is the best way to start.
Nav employee: What geographical area can you work in?
Client: I live in Lillestrøm. I can travel to Oslo, Lørenskog, Strømmen, maybe Gardermoen. I do not have a car right now, so I depend on public transport.
Nav employee: Public transport is important. Gardermoen can be possible for some shifts, but early or late shifts may be difficult. Should we say you can apply within commuting distance by public transport?
Client: Yes. I can start early, but not if the bus or train does not run.
Nav employee: What about shift work?
Client: Day shifts are best. I can do evenings sometimes, but night shifts would be difficult. I did night shifts before, and it affected me a lot.
Nav employee: Then we should mainly look for day work or early evening work. It is better to apply for jobs you can actually keep.
Client: Yes, I agree.
Nav employee: We have already mentioned heavy lifting, public transport, and uncertainty about applications. Is there anything else that makes job searching difficult right now?
Client: Confidence, maybe. After being laid off, I feel less sure of myself. I know it was not my fault, but it still feels like a failure.
Nav employee: Losing a job can affect confidence. We can focus on practical steps that make the process more manageable. Updating the CV, targeting applications, and doing interview preparation can help.
Client: Interview preparation would help. I have not had an interview in many years.
Nav employee: We have job search courses and individual guidance options. Some courses cover CV, applications, interviews, and how to read job advertisements. Would you be interested in a short job search course?
Client: Yes, if it is not too long. I do not want to spend months in a course instead of applying for jobs.
Nav employee: The courses I am thinking of are short. The purpose is to support your job search, not replace it. Another option is that you first update your CV, and then we schedule a follow-up meeting to review it together.
Client: I would like someone to look at the CV before I send more applications.
Nav employee: We can do that. Are you comfortable using the online portal to upload your CV?
Client: I think so. I have used it to send forms, but I have not uploaded documents before.
Nav employee: I can explain the steps before you leave. We can write in the agreement that you upload an updated CV by next Monday. Does that deadline feel realistic?
Client: Next Monday should be possible. I need the weekend to work on it.
Nav employee: Good. Today is Thursday, so Monday gives you a few days. How many targeted applications do you think you can send per week while updating your CV?
Client: Maybe three or four good ones. I can send more if they are simple, but if I have to adapt them, three or four is realistic.
Nav employee: I would rather see three good targeted applications than ten very general ones. Shall we agree on at least three targeted applications per week for relevant jobs?
Client: Yes, that sounds fair.
Nav employee: You can register those applications in your job search log. It helps both you and us see what you have done.
Client: Okay.
Nav employee: You mentioned that you are not confident with Excel. Would you be interested in a short digital skills course if it could help you apply for logistics assistant or order processing roles?
Client: Yes. I am not looking for a long education, but I would like to feel more confident.
Nav employee: Then I can check relevant short courses or guidance options. I cannot promise a specific course today, but I can check what is available and whether it fits your plan.
Client: That would be helpful.
Nav employee: Have you considered temporary work agencies? Many logistics and warehouse jobs are recruited that way.
Client: I have thought about it, but I have not registered with any. I was not sure if it was worth it.
Nav employee: It can be worth it, especially when you already have warehouse experience and forklift certificates. Temporary work can sometimes lead to permanent employment. Would you be willing to register with two or three agencies that work with logistics?
Client: Yes, I can do that.
Nav employee: Then we can include an agreement that you register with at least two staffing agencies that recruit for logistics or inventory jobs by next week.
Client: Yes.
Nav employee: What kind of support do you need from us to do that?
Client: Maybe a list of agencies or websites. I can search myself, but it helps if I know where to start.
Nav employee: I can send you links to relevant job portals and agencies. I will also send information about improving your CV.
Client: Thank you.
Nav employee: Are you comfortable applying and interviewing in Norwegian?
Client: Yes, mostly. I speak Norwegian every day, but I write better in English. Applications in Norwegian take me longer.
Nav employee: Since many job advertisements are in Norwegian, it may be best to have a strong Norwegian CV and application template. We can help make the language clear and professional. It does not need to be complicated.
Client: That would be good. I worry that my writing sounds too simple.
Nav employee: Simple and clear is often best. Employers want to understand what you can do. For example: I have six years of experience from warehouse work and am used to working accurately in a busy environment.
Client: I can write something like that.
Nav employee: Do you have references from your previous employer?
Client: My former team leader said I could use him as a reference. I have his phone number.
Nav employee: Make sure you ask him again before you list him, and write his name, role, company, phone number, and email if you have it.
Client: I will do that.
Nav employee: Have you received written confirmation that you were laid off?
Client: Yes, I have a termination letter. It says the reason was downsizing.
Nav employee: Keep that document. It can be relevant for benefits and for explaining gaps in employment, but you do not need to attach it to ordinary job applications unless an employer asks.
Client: Okay.
Nav employee: Let me summarize what I have understood so far. You were laid off from a warehouse job after six years because the company downsized. You want to return to work and are mainly looking for roles in logistics, inventory, order processing, or related work. You want to avoid constant heavy lifting, you depend on public transport, and you need support with CV, applications, interview preparation, and possibly digital skills. Is that accurate?
Client: Yes, that is accurate.
Nav employee: Is anything important missing?
Client: Maybe that I am stressed about money. I know we do not need to go into details, but it affects me.
Nav employee: It is relevant to understand that financial stress affects your situation. For this work plan, we can write that stable income through work is important and that you are actively applying for jobs while receiving unemployment benefits. We do not need to write private financial details in the meeting summary.
Client: That makes sense.
Nav employee: Do you have concerns about accepting temporary work?
Client: I worry that if I accept short assignments, I might lose benefits or end up with unstable income.
Nav employee: In general, you must report work and hours correctly. Temporary work can affect payments depending on how much you work, but it can also be a good way into employment. Before accepting an assignment, you can check what it means for your reporting. The important thing is to report accurately.
Client: I would consider temporary work if it is relevant and not too physically heavy.
Nav employee: Then we can write that temporary assignments in logistics or inventory work may be relevant if the tasks and travel are suitable.
Client: Yes.
Nav employee: Logistics has openings, but there can be many applicants. If you only apply for the exact same warehouse roles as before, the options may be limited. If we broaden the search to inventory assistant, logistics coordinator assistant, order handler, goods reception, customer service for transport companies, and staffing agencies, you may have more opportunities.
Client: I did not know I could apply for customer service in transport. I thought customer service meant call centers.
Nav employee: Sometimes it does, but transport and logistics companies also need people who understand deliveries, delays, order numbers, and warehouse routines. Your practical background can help.
Client: I did that sometimes at the warehouse. I spoke with drivers and checked delivery problems.
Nav employee: Then that should go in your CV. Not just packing orders, but communication with drivers, handling delivery deviations, and solving practical issues.
Client: I never thought of that as a skill.
Nav employee: It is a skill. Employers need people who can solve everyday problems. You should also mention training new employees. That shows responsibility.
Client: Okay.
Nav employee: If an employer asks why you left your last job, what would you say?
Client: I would say the company downsized and several people were laid off.
Nav employee: That is a good answer. Keep it short and neutral. You can add that you are now looking for a role where you can use your logistics experience in a sustainable way.
Client: Sustainable meaning not too heavy?
Nav employee: Yes, but in an interview you can phrase it positively: I am looking for a role where I can use my warehouse and logistics experience, especially inventory control, order handling, and coordination.
Client: That sounds better.
Nav employee: If an employer asks about physical tasks, answer honestly but focus on what you can do. For example: I can do active work and normal warehouse tasks, but I am looking for a role that is not mainly heavy lifting all day.
Client: Yes, that is honest.
Nav employee: Let us set a follow-up meeting. Would two weeks from now be useful? That gives you time to update your CV, apply for jobs, and register with agencies.
Client: Two weeks sounds good.
Nav employee: I have an available slot on Wednesday at 10:00. Would that work?
Client: Yes, Wednesday at 10 works.
Nav employee: Good. Before that meeting, you will upload an updated CV, send at least three targeted applications per week, register with at least two staffing agencies, and check the online portal weekly. I will send links to relevant job portals, information about CV writing, and check whether a short digital skills course is available. Is that correct?
Client: Yes, that is correct.
Nav employee: Do you feel the plan is realistic?
Client: Yes. It feels like a lot, but it is manageable because it is specific. I know what to do first.
Nav employee: What will you do first when you get home?
Client: I will open my CV and add more details about the warehouse system, forklift certificates, training new employees, and communication with drivers. Then I will ask my old team leader if I can use him as a reference.
Nav employee: That sounds like a good first step. After that, you can look at job advertisements and adapt the CV or application to each one.
Client: Yes.
Nav employee: Is there anything you are worried about in the plan?
Client: Maybe the applications. I am afraid I will still write them badly.
Nav employee: Use the job advertisement as a guide. If it says they need someone accurate, give an example of accuracy. If it says they need forklift experience, make that visible. Save the applications you send, and we can review one or two in the next meeting.
Client: That would help.
Nav employee: I will include in the meeting summary that we will review applications next time. The summary will focus on your work goal, what we discussed, and what we agreed.
Client: That is good.
Nav employee: Do you have any questions before we finish?
Client: Just one. If I find a part-time job, should I apply?
Nav employee: Yes, if it is relevant and realistic. Part-time work can be a step toward full-time work. You should report any work correctly if you start working while receiving benefits. Relevant part-time work can strengthen your CV and network.
Client: Okay. I will include part-time jobs if they are relevant.
Nav employee: What about jobs outside logistics, for example retail or customer service?
Client: I am open to retail if it is not too much heavy lifting. I have some customer contact experience, but not from a shop.
Nav employee: Then retail stockroom, goods reception in stores, or customer service linked to deliveries could be relevant. We can include that as a secondary direction.
Client: Yes, that makes sense.
Nav employee: I will write that your main goal is logistics and inventory-related work, with retail stockroom or delivery-related customer service as possible alternatives.
Client: That sounds accurate.
Nav employee: I will summarize the agreements one last time. You update and upload your CV by Monday. You send at least three targeted applications each week. You register with at least two relevant staffing agencies. You check the online portal weekly. I send links and check short digital skills options. At the next meeting, we review the CV, applications, and job search progress. Next meeting is Wednesday at 10:00.
Client: Yes. That is clear.
Nav employee: I will send the meeting summary after this meeting. Please read it when you receive it. If something is wrong or unclear, contact me.
Client: I will. Thank you for explaining everything. I feel a bit calmer now.
Nav employee: I am glad to hear that. You have useful experience, and the plan now is to present it more clearly and apply for roles that fit your situation. We will follow up in two weeks.
Client: Thank you. See you then.
Nav employee: See you then, and good luck with the CV work.
